prompt: You need to chart revenue for 18 products whose names run to thirty characters. Which form fits?

choices.text: Horizontal bars
choices.why: Right. Bars give every long name the whole margin, set level.

choices.text: Vertical columns with the labels tilted to fit
choices.why: Tilted labels are slower to read, and with eighteen of them nearly unreadable.

choices.text: A pie with eighteen slices
choices.why: Lesson 2 says five slices at most.

choices.text: Columns with the names in a legend instead
choices.why: A legend makes the reader match eighteen colours to eighteen names.

prompt: When does a column chart suit the data better than a bar chart?

choices.text: When there are many categories with long names
choices.why: That is exactly when bars win.

choices.text: When the values are close together and the differences are hard to see
choices.why: Columns and bars show differences equally; the orientation does not change that.

choices.text: When the categories are months
choices.why: Right. Time runs left to right, so columns read as a sequence.

choices.text: When the chart is a ranking
choices.why: A ranking reads best top to bottom, as bars.

prompt: Somebody removes the gaps between the bars of an ordinary bar chart to make it look tidier. What will readers tend to assume?

choices.text: That the chart is more precise
choices.why: Precision does not change; what changes is what the chart seems to be.

choices.text: That it is a histogram of one continuous quantity
choices.why: Right. Touching bars are the histogram's signature.

choices.text: That the bars are sorted
choices.why: Gaps have nothing to do with order.

choices.text: Nothing; the gaps carry no meaning
choices.why: The gaps say the categories are separate.

prompt: Software draws a bar chart of five regions in alphabetical order. What is the usual fix?

choices.text: Sort by value
choices.why: Right. Sorted, the ranking is the picture.

choices.text: Reverse the alphabetical order
choices.why: Still an order that has nothing to do with the question.

choices.text: Colour the bars from light to dark by name
choices.why: That adds an order to the colours that the names do not have.

choices.text: Leave it, since readers look names up alphabetically
choices.why: Looking a name up is what a table is for. A chart is for comparing.

prompt: A column chart shows orders for each hour of the day, 8:00 to 22:00. Should the columns be sorted by value?

choices.text: Yes, largest first, as with any bar chart
choices.why: Sort by value only when the categories have no order.

choices.text: No: the hours have an order of their own, and it wins
choices.why: Right. Sorting would destroy the daily rhythm the reader is looking for.

choices.text: Yes, but smallest first
choices.why: The direction is not the issue; sorting itself breaks the sequence.

choices.text: Only if there are more than twelve hours
choices.why: The number of categories does not change whether they have an order.

prompt: Where does an "Other" bar belong, after the small categories are merged into it?

choices.text: Last, whatever its size
choices.why: Right. It is not a category like the rest.

choices.text: In its place by value, like any other bar
choices.why: Then a large Other in second place reads as a real category.

choices.text: First, so the reader sees how much was merged
choices.why: First place is the most read; it should go to the largest real category.

choices.text: Nowhere; Other should be dropped
choices.why: Dropping it hides part of the total.

prompt: Northeast had 39,924 orders and South 34,926. With the axis starting at 34,000, how many times South's visible height is Northeast's? Answer to one decimal place.
hint: Subtract the floor from both before dividing.

prompt: Why must the value axis of a bar chart start at zero?

choices.text: Spreadsheets refuse to draw it any other way
choices.why: Many draw it any way you like, and some pick a non-zero start on their own.

choices.text: Because negative values might appear later in the year
choices.why: Negative values are a separate matter; the reason is about length.

choices.text: The bar's length is the number
choices.why: Right. Cut the base and the length stops being the number.

choices.text: A style guide requires it
choices.why: It is not a matter of style. It is the encoding.

prompt: A difference between two bars is real but too small to see from zero. Which of these show it honestly? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Write the numbers beside bars that start at zero
choices.why: Right. The reader gets the exact difference without a distorted picture.

choices.text: Start the bar axis just below the smaller value
choices.why: That is the truncated axis.

choices.text: Plot the difference itself, from zero
choices.why: Right. The gap becomes the bar.

choices.text: Use a dot plot, whose axis may start anywhere
choices.why: Right. A dot is a position, not a length.

prompt: A line chart of daily temperature runs from 18 to 24 degrees, with its axis from 18 to 24. Is that the same mistake as a truncated bar chart?

choices.text: Yes: every chart's axis must start at zero
choices.why: The rule belongs to marks whose length or area carries the number.

choices.text: Yes, unless the temperatures are in Fahrenheit
choices.why: The unit does not change what the mark encodes.

choices.text: No, because temperatures are categories
choices.why: Temperatures are quantities. The reason is that a line is read by position.

choices.text: No: a line encodes position, so its axis fits the data
choices.why: Right. Nothing is read as a length from a base.

prompt: One region's bar is so large that the others are squashed near the axis. What does the lesson suggest instead of breaking the large bar?

choices.text: A zigzag on the large bar
choices.why: That is the break, which still makes the reader compare lengths that are not the numbers.

choices.text: A second chart, or a logarithmic dot plot
choices.why: Right. Both keep every mark honest.

choices.text: Starting the axis at the smallest value
choices.why: That truncates every bar.

choices.text: Removing the large region from the data
choices.why: Hiding the largest value changes the story.

prompt: In a stacked bar, which segment can the reader compare accurately across bars?

choices.text: The top one
choices.why: It starts wherever the segments below it ended.

choices.text: The bottom one
choices.why: Right. It is the only one sitting on the common baseline.

choices.text: The largest one, wherever it sits
choices.why: Size does not help if its starting point moves.

choices.text: Every segment, equally well
choices.why: Only the bottom one shares a start with its counterparts.

prompt: The reader needs to see whether Northeast passed South between 2024 and 2025. Which chart serves them?

choices.text: Grouped bars by region and year
choices.why: Right. Every column starts at zero, so any part compares with any other.

choices.text: A stacked bar per year with the regions inside
choices.why: Northeast and South would float at different heights in each stack.

choices.text: Two pies, one per year
choices.why: Two pies is the worst comparison lesson 2 names.

choices.text: A 100% stacked bar per year
choices.why: It shows shares, and the two regions would still float.

prompt: A stacked bar shows total revenue per quarter, split into four product lines, and the director cares most about Drinks. Where should Drinks go?

choices.text: At the top, where it is most visible
choices.why: Visible is not comparable; the top segment floats.

choices.text: In a brighter colour, wherever it falls
choices.why: Colour draws the eye but cannot fix a moving baseline.

choices.text: At the bottom of every bar
choices.why: Right. The bottom segment is the only one read against a common baseline.

choices.text: In the middle, so it is framed by the others
choices.why: The middle is the hardest place to compare.

prompt: Each group splits into seven parts. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Several small charts, one per part, sharing an axis
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10 is about these small multiples.

choices.text: Grouped bars with seven bars per group
choices.why: Seven bars per group become a comb.

choices.text: Stacked bars with seven segments
choices.why: Six of the seven would float.

choices.text: A pie per group
choices.why: Seven slices, times the number of groups.

prompt: truncated.py printed 1.14 in the data and 6.40 on the page. What lie factor does that give, to one decimal place?
hint: Compare the size of the effect: subtract 1 from each before dividing.

prompt: grouped.py printed "y axis from 0.0". What does that say about matplotlib's bar charts?

choices.text: They always fit the axis tightly around the data
choices.why: A tight fit would have started near 7,000, the smallest value.

choices.text: They cannot be truncated
choices.why: truncated.py truncated one in a single line.

choices.text: They start at zero unless somebody asks otherwise
choices.why: Right. truncated.py had to call set_ylim to cut it.

choices.text: The data contained a zero
choices.why: No region had zero orders; the base comes from the bars.

prompt: Find each of these in the column chart.

labels.text: the value where the axis starts, which should be zero
a label tilted to fit under its column
a gap saying the categories are separate

hint: The axis is numbered on the left.

prompt: Match each need to the chart that serves it.

pairs.left: compare the totals of the groups
rank eighteen products with long names

prompt: Put the checks in the order the lesson recommends making them on a bar chart you are handed.
items: Find the bottom of the value axis
Read what the length means from the axis label
Read the order of the bars
trap: If the base is not zero, every comparison after it is wrong, so it comes first.

prompt: A bar sitting on its side along a vertical baseline is a bar; one standing up from a horizontal baseline is a ___.
